There’s a lot less shame sitting underneath everything now. We both grew up hearing some version of *too sensitive, too intense, too dramatic, too annoying, too much*. Now we work WITH those parts - the intensity became devotion, and the sensitivity transformed into intuition, while the obsession became depth🔥🔥🔥 Just two best friends wildly supporting the shit out of each other, making room for each other’s brains, and feeling very lucky that somehow, in this enormous world, we found someone who feels like home. title: There’s something that I wish every parent, and honestly, every thera...
description: There’s something that I wish every parent, and honestly, every therapist, teacher, pediatrician, and anyone who works with kids, understood: Your child already knows they’re different. Long before anyone says the word autism. Long before anyone says ADHD. Long before anyone suggests an evaluation. They know. They know they’re working harder than everyone else. They know friendships feel harder. They know they’re always being corrected. They know they’re trying so hard to fit in. The only question is what story they’ll tell themselves about why. If we don’t give children the real explanation, they create their own: “I’m weird.” “I’m lazy.” “Something is wrong with me.” “I’m just bad at being a person.” “I don’t belong in this world” And that story doesn’t disappear when they grow up. Often, it intensifies year after year. It’s the same story I hear repeatedly from my fellow neurodivergent adults. It’s also why I get concerned when we stop at “highly sensitive,” “deep feeling,” or “big feeler” without asking whether there could be something more going on. Sometimes those descriptions fit. Often, they’re the beginning of a conversation, not the end of one. This week, a middle school social worker sent me a message I’ll never forget. She asked one of her students why he’d seemed so much happier after receiving his autism diagnosis. He said: “Because now everyone understands what I always knew about me... and I know it’s not my fault.” A diagnosis doesn’t make a child feel different. It gives them the words to understand themselves before shame gets there first. And if you’re struggling with your big feeler, sensitive, intense kid right now, and everything feels like a fit or explosion - let’s get them the tools that will help them the self-awareness, emotional skills, and regulation tools they need to thrive. If you’ve been stuck in the yelling → guilt →  more bad behavior → more yelling cycle… this is your sign to do it differently, and with brain science by your side. title: Being diagnosed autistic left me with two all-consuming, polar opposi...
description: Being diagnosed autistic left me with two all-consuming, polar opposite experiences happening at the exact same time: Utter relief - because my entire life suddenly made sense. My childhood, all my relationships, my career choices - all clicked into place. All the things I’d felt so broken for, for so long, suddenly felt like i was allowed to love them. And at the exact same time, i started to completely mentally unravel… Skill regression, which can happen to a lot of late-diagnosed autistics right after diagnosis. Realizing I’d been living in autistic burnout for a long time (which is a very specific burnout experience). And complete + terrifying loss of identity - because I’d been trying so hard to push through, be less sensitive, override my nervous system, talk like everyone else, be relatable, be less blunt/jarring - for sooo long, that i actually didn’t know who i was any longer. It’s a really scary place to be. i decided to share it all in this week’s substack. Read the full free article at the link in bio or on the substack app. 🫶 It’s a really personal one for me, and if it helps even just one person while they’re feeling lost in their own journey, then it’ll feel completely worth sharing.
